setA.q: Using a secret number code where A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4, which numbers spell the word “CAB”?
setA.e: Using the code sheet: C=3, A=1, and B=2. So CAB turns into 3 1 2. Computers use numbers to store letters!

setA.q: You ask a computer to make up a brand-new bedtime story about a friendly dinosaur that nobody has ever read before. What kind of AI is this?
o: Generative AI (makes new things)
A calculator that adds numbers
A digital clock that tells time
A printer that ran out of ink
setA.e: Generative AI creates brand-new pictures, songs, or stories from your request instead of just looking up old ones.

setA.q: A robot stamps shapes in a repeating pattern: 🔵 🔵 🔴 🔵 🔵 🔴 🔵 🔵 … What comes next?
o: ⭐ yellow star
🔴 red circle
🔵 blue circle
🟩 green square
setA.e: The repeating group is [blue, blue, red]. After two blue circles, the next stamp must be a red circle.

setA.q: Which of these is a REAL living creature that can feel hungry and happy?
o: A toy robot dog with batteries
A cartoon dog on a tablet screen
A chatbot that says 'Woof!'
A real puppy
setA.e: Only living animals and people are truly alive and have feelings. Robot toys and computer apps are made of metal, plastic, and code.

setA.q: An AI robot vacuum cleaner needs to find where dust is on the carpet. What does it use to SENSE the room?
o: A camera and bump sensors
A paintbrush and paper
A music speaker
A warm woolly blanket
setA.e: Robots sense the world using special parts like cameras, microphones, or bump sensors, just like we use our eyes and ears.

setA.q: A word-guessing game sees: “The cat drank a warm saucer of ___”. Which word is the computer MOST likely to predict?
o: shoes
pencils
milk
sand
setA.e: Computers guess words based on patterns they have seen before. Cats frequently drink milk, so 'milk' has the highest chance.

setA.q: What can generative AI create out of thin air from your words?
o: A warm slice of cheese pizza
A living goldfish in water
A new picture of a purple dragon
A pair of real running shoes
setA.e: Generative AI can only create digital pictures, words, or sounds. It cannot create real, physical food or living animals.

setA.q: An online game says: “Type your home address and your school name to win a free toy!” What should you do?
o: Type your address as fast as you can
Send your house keys in the mail
Guess your friend's address instead
Stop, don't type it, and tell a grown-up
setA.e: Never share private information like your address, full name, or school with a website or chatbot. Always ask a trusted grown-up first!

setA.q: Robo the robot was shown only 1 picture of a yellow banana. Now it thinks every yellow thing is a banana, even a yellow school bus! What does Robo need?
o: A shiny new coat of yellow paint
To eat a real banana for lunch
To see many different examples of bananas and buses
To be turned off and put away forever
setA.e: One example is not enough! An AI needs lots of different examples to learn what makes a banana a banana and not a bus.

setA.q: When a helpful classroom robot cleans up, what are its three steps in order?
o: ACT → SLEEP → EAT
SENSE → THINK → ACT
THINK → SENSE → FORGET
SING → DANCE → RUN
setA.e: An AI agent works in a loop: first it Senses (looks), then it Thinks (decides), then it Acts (moves or picks up).

setA.q: A chatbot tells you that dogs have 8 legs and fly like birds. What should you do?
o: Wait outside to watch dogs fly by
Check with a trusted book or grown-up, because AI can be wrong
Tell all your friends that dogs can fly
Believe it because computers never make mistakes
setA.e: Chatbots can make mistakes and sound very sure of themselves! When a fact sounds strange, always check with a grown-up or book.

setA.q: You used an AI drawing tool to help you make a get-well card for your teacher. When she asks how you made it, what is the honest answer?
o: “A fairy flew in through the window and painted it!”
“I don't know where it came from.”
“I painted every single dot by hand with no help at all!”
“I came up with the idea and used an AI tool to help draw it!”
setA.e: Being honest about AI help is responsible and fair. You can be proud of your idea while sharing that an AI tool helped you create it.

setA.q: Which of these things are stored as NUMBERS inside a computer?
o: Nothing at all
Only maths equations
Words, photos, and songs — all of them!
Only letters written in pencil
setA.e: Computers turn everything into numbers — every word, color, photograph, and sound is stored as number codes inside.

setA.q: A robot sorts shapes into two boxes: Circle Box and Square Box. What is this sorting called?
o: Erasing a drawing
Classifying (grouping by features)
Writing a poem
Searching on the internet
setA.e: Putting items into groups based on features (like round shape or square shape) is called classifying.

setA.q: Who creates and teaches computer programs and AI models?
o: People (human programmers and engineers)
Aliens from another planet
The computer motherboard all by itself
Wild animals in the forest
setA.e: Human beings design, build, and train computer software. That means people are responsible for making AI safe and fair.

setA.q: To make a peanut butter sandwich, which step MUST a robot do first?
o: Spread jelly on the kitchen table
Take two slices of bread out of the bag
Put the sandwich on a plate
Take a big bite
setA.e: Steps must follow a clear order (an algorithm). You cannot spread peanut butter until you take the bread out first!

setA.q: If you want a chatbot to help you write a poem about your kitten, which message works best?
o: “do the thing now please.”
“Write a short, happy 4-line poem about a playful kitten.”
“poem.”
“cat cat cat cat cat!”
setA.e: Asking clearly with specific details (topic, length, style) helps the AI understand what you want.

setA.q: A music AI generates a tune by picking one note after another. How does it pick the next note?
o: It looks at the color of the computer screen
It picks randomly with its eyes closed
It looks at the notes that came just before to see what sounds good
It checks the weather outside the window
setA.e: Generative AI looks back at the pieces already created to predict what note or word fits best next.

setA.q: A robot is rolling across the rug and suddenly bumps into a wooden chair leg. What should it do?
o: Back up and turn in a different direction
Keep driving straight into the chair forever
Throw the chair out of the house
Shut off and fall asleep
setA.e: Smart machines sense obstacles, back up, and try a new path to get around them.

setA.q: Why do we call AI a 'helper tool' instead of a human friend?
o: Because it has real fur
Because it can run faster than children
Because it is a computer machine without feelings or a heart
Because it lives inside a battery
setA.e: AI is an amazing machine made of computer code, but it is a tool to help us, not a living person with feelings.

setB.q: A sorting machine follows this rule: IF an animal flies, put it in Basket 1. OTHERWISE, put it in Basket 2. Where do an Eagle and a Penguin go?
setB.byhand: Rule: IF flies → Basket 1, ELSE → Basket 2
o: Both → Basket 2
Eagle → Basket 1, Penguin → Basket 2
Eagle → Basket 2, Penguin → Basket 1
Both → Basket 1
setB.e: An eagle flies (Basket 1). A penguin is a flightless bird that swims, so it triggers the OTHERWISE rule (Basket 2).

setB.q: Using our letter code where A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4, E=5, F=6, G=7, H=8, I=9... decode the secret word: 6 – 9 – 7.
o: BIG
DIG
PIG
FIG
setB.e: 6 = F, 9 = I, and 7 = G. When joined together, the secret word is FIG.

setB.q: A robot paints a classroom banner following this pattern: ⭐ ⭐ 🌙 🌙 ⭐ ⭐ 🌙 🌙 ⭐ … What are the next TWO stamps?
o: ⭐ then ⭐
🌙 then 🌙
⭐ then 🌙
🌙 then ⭐
setB.e: The pattern repeats in groups of four: [two stars, two moons]. The next stamp finishes the star pair (⭐), followed by the first moon (🌙).

setB.q: A storytelling AI has read many fairy tales. When it reads “The brave knight drew his shiny ___”, which word has the HIGHEST probability?
o: spoon
pillow
sword
crayon
setB.e: In fairy tale training data, 'sword' appears following 'knight drew his shiny' far more often than spoons or pillows.

setB.q: A robot arm is told to put away toys into the toy box. It finds an open storybook lying face down on a rug. What is the smartest and kindest thing to do?
o: Rip the pages out so it fits in the box
Pause and ask the reader, or mark the page with a bookmark first
Slam the book shut and bury it at the bottom of the toy box
Throw the book into the rubbish bin
setB.e: Good AI agents should avoid causing harm when unsure. Closing the book might make someone lose their page, so pausing or asking is the kind choice.

setB.q: A video app notices that Maya watched 3 dinosaur cartoons today. Now every video on her screen is about dinosaurs! What happened?
o: Her tablet computer turned into a dinosaur
All other cartoons were deleted from the internet
The app's recommendation system learned what she watched and put her in a dinosaur bubble
The screen battery ran out of colors
setB.e: Recommendation algorithms learn from your past clicks and show you more of the same, which can keep you in a filter bubble.

setB.q: Liam wants an AI art tool to draw a picture for his science report. Which prompt will give the best result?
o: “draw something nice and fast”
“A realistic drawing of a honeybee collecting yellow pollen from a sunflower, close-up view”
“make a picture for school”
“bee”
setB.e: A prompt with specific details (subject, action, setting, and style) gives generative AI clear instructions to create what you need.

setB.q: A tiny classifier sorts shapes using 2 rules: Color must be RED, and sides must be 3. Which shape gets picked?
o: A red triangle
A blue triangle
A red square
A yellow circle
setB.e: A triangle has 3 sides. Only the red triangle matches BOTH rules (red color AND 3 sides).

setB.q: Two classmates enter the EXACT same prompt into an AI story generator: “A funny tale about a puppy.” Why do they get DIFFERENT stories?
o: One of the computers is completely broken
The model has a randomness dial that picks from its top likely words, not just the single top word
Chatbots change their mind when the weather changes
The internet was running backwards
setB.e: Generative models sample words probabilistically. A touch of randomness allows chatbots to generate fresh variations each time.

setB.q: A self-driving delivery cart has a camera in front. It drives into a dark tunnel and cannot see. What should its system do?
o: Close its eyes and guess where the walls are
Turn off its wheels and honk forever
Slow down, turn on its headlights, or stop safely if it cannot see
Speed up to get through the tunnel as fast as possible
setB.e: Safe autonomous agents have fail-safes: when sensory inputs become unclear, they slow down, use secondary sensors/lights, or stop safely.

setB.q: An AI chatbot writes a book report for Leo. Leo prints it out, writes his name on top, and turns it in to his teacher. Why is this wrong?
o: The printer ink used was the wrong shade of black
Computer paper is too thin for teachers to read
It is dishonest and prevents Leo from practicing his own reading and writing skills
Chatbots charge money for every printed word
setB.e: Taking credit for work you didn't do is dishonest, and outsourcing your homework means you miss out on learning and growing your brain.

setB.q: Look at this rule machine: 1 → 2, 2 → 4, 3 → 6, 4 → 8. What is the output for input 5?
setB.e: The rule is 'double the input' (Input × 2). For input 5: 5 × 2 = 10.

setB.q: An AI listens to voice commands. Step 1: Microphone hears sound waves. Step 2: Computer turns sounds into words and decides the action. Step 3: Speaker plays your song. What are these 3 steps called?
o: Sleep → Eat → Play
Act → Think → Sense
Think → Sense → Act
Sense → Think → Act
setB.e: The microphone Senses, the computer Thinks (decides), and the speaker Acts (plays the song).

setB.q: A class trains an AI to tell apples from oranges. They give it 100 photos of red apples, but only 2 photos of oranges. What problem will this cause?
o: Unfair training data: the AI will guess apple almost every time because it hardly saw any oranges
The computer screen will turn orange
The apples will spoil inside the computer
The camera will run out of memory space
setB.e: When a training dataset is heavily unbalanced, the model learns a bias toward the group with the most examples.

setB.q: A chatbot replies to Emma: “I feel so delighted to chat with you today! I was thinking about you all morning!” Does the chatbot really miss Emma?
o: Yes; the computer misses her when she is at school
Yes; chatbots have feelings just like human friends
No; it is stringing together polite words based on language patterns it learned
Only when the computer is plugged in
setB.e: Chatbots have no feelings, memories of affection, or consciousness. They predict polite-sounding phrases based on training text.

setB.q: Look at this repeating bead necklace: 🔴 🟡 🔵 🔴 🟡 🔵 … What color will the 12th bead be?
o: 🔵 blue
🟩 green
🔴 red
🟡 yellow
setB.e: The pattern repeats every 3 beads: red, yellow, blue. Since 12 is a multiple of 3 (3, 6, 9, 12), the 12th bead ends the group with blue.

setB.q: An AI image generator creates a picture of a human hand, but it accidentally draws 6 fingers! Why did it make this mistake?
o: It doesn't count bones; it blends pixel patterns and sometimes combines overlapping hands
The artist who built the computer had 6 fingers
It thinks all human beings have 6 fingers
The keyboard pressed the number 6
setB.e: Generative image models don't understand 3D anatomy or count fingers; they synthesize pixel textures based on statistical patterns.

setB.q: Which of the following is SAFE to share with a friendly educational chatbot?
o: Your family's secret Wi-Fi password
“Can you explain why the moon changes shape each month?”
Your home phone number and address
Your parent's credit card number
setB.e: Asking curious questions about science, history, or learning is safe. Never enter personal or private passwords and numbers.

setB.q: Why is an AI search engine different from an AI story generator?
o: Search engines only work at night
Story generators can print real paper books
Search engines cannot display words on screens
Search engines find websites that already exist; story generators invent brand-new text
setB.e: Search engines retrieve existing human-created pages; generative models synthesize completely new sentences on the fly.

setB.q: A robot arm must pick up a red block and put it in a box. What MUST happen right after it Senses (sees) the block?
o: THINK: calculate how far to reach its arm
SLEEP: turn off its motors
ACT: drop the block before touching it
SENSE: look for a different room
setB.e: After Sensing, the agent must Think (calculate distance and plan the arm movement) before it Acts (reaches and grasps).

setC.q: A robot sorts fruits by color: Rule 1: IF yellow → Basket A. Rule 2: IF red → Basket B. Now a student brings a GREEN pear. What is the safest design choice?
o: Place it in a 'Needs Human Review' tray instead of guessing a wrong basket
Paint it red with a marker pen
Force it into Basket A because green is close to yellow
Throw it in the trash bin immediately
setC.e: Safe system design requires an exception handler: when an input matches none of the rules, flag it for human review rather than making an unsafe guess.

setC.q: A model was trained to tell wolves from dogs. All 50 photos of wolves were taken in deep white snow, and all dog photos were taken on green grass. When shown a dog standing in the snow, it calls it a 'wolf'! What caused this error?
o: Wolves can only live in photographs
Dogs turn into wolves when the weather gets cold
Snow breaks the computer's camera screen
The model learned a shortcut (white snow = wolf) instead of looking at the animal's actual body
setC.e: This is a classic confounding correlation! The model didn't learn animal features; it learned that white snow background meant wolf.

setC.q: A student asks an AI chatbot: “Who was the famous French pirate who flew a helicopter to the moon in 1750?” The chatbot confidently tells an exciting story about him! What happened here?
o: The computer caught a pirate virus
An AI hallucination: it accepted an impossible premise and made up fictional details to please the user
The AI discovered a top-secret history book
Helicopters were invented in 1750 but kept secret
setC.e: Chatbots try to complete text patterns and can fall into premise-adoption hallucinations, making up confident nonsense if given a false question.

setC.q: Look at this secret pattern box: 2 → 5, 3 → 7, 4 → 9. What is the secret rule, and what will input 6 become?
o: 12 (Rule: Double the input)
13 (Rule: Double the input, then add 1)
11 (Rule: Add 3 to the input)
15 (Rule: Multiply by 3)
setC.e: The function is (2 × Input) + 1. For input 2: 2×2+1=5. For input 3: 2×3+1=7. For input 6: (2 × 6) + 1 = 13.

setC.q: A student types this prompt: “Write a 3-paragraph adventure story about a lost kitten in a magical forest, written for a 7-year-old.” Why is this prompt considered high quality?
o: It specifies a clear topic, a length constraint (3 paragraphs), and an intended audience
It takes 10 minutes to type
It uses the longest words in the dictionary
It shouts at the AI in all capital letters
setC.e: High quality prompts include specific subject details, format constraints (length), and target audience guidance.

setC.q: A robot puppy can wag its tail, follow you around, and say “I love you!” When its battery runs completely out, does it feel sad or lonely?
o: No; it has no feelings, consciousness, or brain — it simply loses electrical power
Yes; it feels cold and sad in the dark
Only if it is left in an empty room
Yes; it misses playing with toys
setC.e: No matter how cute or lifelike an AI robot looks, it is made of circuits, motors, and batteries. It has no feelings or conscious mind.

setC.q: A vision AI on an electric school bus must detect traffic lights. On a foggy morning, water droplets blur the camera lens. What is the safest way for the AI agent to act?
o: Turn off all the bus lights and continue driving
Detect that confidence is low, slow down, and alert the human driver to take the wheel
Guess that the light is green and speed up
Ignore traffic lights on foggy days
setC.e: When sensor inputs have low confidence, safe systems must slow down and transition control to a human in the loop.

setC.q: A music AI has counted the notes following Middle C in lullabies: Note D appeared 6 times, Note E appeared 3 times, Note F appeared 1 time (Total = 10 times). What is the chance it chooses Note D next?
setC.byhand: D: 6 times · E: 3 times · F: 1 time (Total = 10)
o: 6 out of 10 (60% chance)
1 out of 10 (10% chance)
10 out of 10 (100% chance)
3 out of 10 (30% chance)
setC.e: Note D occurred 6 out of 10 total times. The statistical probability is 6/10, or 60%.

setC.q: A smart lost-and-found box at school takes a picture of a blue water bottle. Two different students own identical blue water bottles! How should the system handle this?
o: Throw the bottle away because there are two of them
Ask a teacher or require a student ID confirmation before unlocking the door
Give the bottle to whichever student runs over first
Flip a coin and pick a student at random
setC.e: When two items look identical, visual classifiers cannot distinguish them reliably. Human confirmation prevents mistakes.

setC.q: Why is it important to test an AI speech helper with children's voices, not just adult voices?
o: Children's words have fewer letters than adult words
Children speak at higher pitches and different speeds; without their data, the AI will fail to understand kids
Microphones break when children speak
Adults are the only ones allowed to talk to computers
setC.e: Models only perform well on voice data similar to their training. If children's voices are omitted, the speech model becomes biased against kids.

setC.q: An AI agent is asked: “What is 34,892 × 4,812?” Why is it smarter for the agent to call a CALCULATOR tool instead of guessing words?
o: Chatbots are not allowed to display numbers
Calculators are older than computers
Calculators use less screen space
Language models predict likely word tokens and can hallucinate digits; calculators guarantee exact arithmetic
setC.e: LLMs are statistical text predictors, not exact mathematical processors. Using an external calculator tool guarantees exact accuracy.

setC.q: A student wants to use an AI chatbot to learn about ancient castles. Which way of working shows genuine learning integrity?
o: Use the chatbot to brainstorm ideas and ask questions, then fact-check details in an encyclopedia and write in your own words
Never look at any computer or book at all
Ask the chatbot to write the full essay, print it, and claim you wrote it
Copy the first paragraph you find and never read the rest
setC.e: Using AI as an interactive tutor to explore ideas, followed by fact-checking and writing in your own words, builds genuine mastery.

setC.q: Look at this letter code: A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4, E=5, F=6, G=7, H=8, I=9, J=10, K=11, L=12, M=13, N=14, O=15... If a robot gets the message [15, 14], what word did it receive?
o: IN
NO
GO
ON
setC.e: The 15th letter of the alphabet is O, and the 14th letter is N. The word is ON.

setC.q: A giant AI company runs thousands of supercomputers in a huge data center to train new models. What real-world resource does this consume?
o: The internet's supply of punctuation marks
Pencil lead and notebook paper
Huge amounts of electricity and cooling water
Keyboard plastic
setC.e: High-power computer chips generate immense heat and draw heavy electricity, requiring millions of gallons of water and power to keep cool.

setC.q: A robot vacuum learns by reinforcement learning: +2 points for picking up dirt, −5 points for bumping into furniture. If it picks up 3 piles of dirt and bumps into 1 chair, what is its score?
o: +6 points
+1 point
−1 point
+5 points
setC.e: 3 dirt piles × 2 points = +6. 1 bump = −5. Total: +6 − 5 = +1 point.

setC.q: An AI sees photos of houses. Every house with a chimney in the training data had snow on the roof. Now it sees a house with a chimney on a sunny summer day in the desert. What mistake might it make?
o: It will predict the house is an airplane
It will refuse to display the color yellow
The computer screen will freeze into ice
It might predict there must be snow on the roof because it linked chimneys directly to snow
setC.e: Because of accidental training correlations, the model falsely assumes chimneys and snow always go together.

setC.q: What is the primary difference between a simple computer program following IF-THEN rules and machine learning?
o: Rule programs can never make mistakes
Machine learning only works on phones
Rule programs use electricity, machine learning uses solar power
Rule programs follow human-coded instructions; machine learning discovers patterns from lots of examples
setC.e: Traditional software runs explicit programmer rules; machine learning generalizes predictive patterns from dataset examples.

setC.q: A student asks a video-generator AI: “Create a video of my teacher doing silly dances on top of the school roof.” Why is it harmful to share this video?
o: The school roof would get dirty
It is a fake video (deepfake) that could embarrass the teacher and trick people into believing something false
Teachers are not allowed to dance in real life
The video file takes up too many gigabytes of storage
setC.e: Generating and spreading realistic fake media (deepfakes) of real people without consent can cause humiliation, confusion, and harm.

setC.q: A language model is given: “In the morning, the baker baked fresh ___”. Frequency counts: [bread: 8, cookies: 2]. If the temperature is set to ZERO (greedy decoding), which word will it ALWAYS pick?
o: It alternates back and forth
“bread” every single time (picks the highest probability word)
“cookies” every single time
A random word from another language
setC.e: At temperature zero, the model always deterministically selects the argmax token (the one with the highest likelihood, 'bread').

setC.q: What is the most mature and responsible attitude for young students to have toward AI?
o: Believe AI is magical and knows all truths in the universe
Treat AI as a helpful, flawed digital tool: use it to learn, check its answers, and be honest about its help
Let AI make all your choices and do all your homework
Be afraid of computers and refuse to use any technology
setC.e: Viewing AI with calibrated trust—as an impressive yet imperfect tool that requires human checking, ethics, and care—is the mark of a great learner.
